whatToDoNext: You can sue for money owed under an agreement, like an unpaid loan, or goods or services that were not paid for. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. yourDeadline:
The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
whatHappensAfter: Court staff review online filings within 3 business days. You cannot file online to meet a deadline that is 3 business days away or less. userQuestion: I was hurt by a car, truck or bus — is there something I have to do before I sue?
whatsHappening: This is about an injury or a death that came, directly or indirectly, from the use or operation of an automobile. The law lists six things to be done before this kind of lawsuit is started. You must always do three of them. You only have to do the other three if the person you plan to sue asks. The first two are to apply for statutory accident benefits and to serve a written notice that you plan to sue. The others are below. If you do not do one or more of these six things, you can still sue. But the court must take that into account when it decides costs.
whatToDoNext: Apply for statutory accident benefits. Also serve a written notice on the person you plan to sue, saying that you plan to sue them. You must serve this notice within 120 days after the incident. The court where the lawsuit could be started can allow more time. You ask by motion, before or after the 120 days run out. There are rules for how the notice must be served, in section 33 of the Insurance Act. The notice must tell that person that, if they are insured, they must give their insurer a copy within seven days of getting it. You must also give the person you plan to sue the information the regulations require, by the deadline the regulations set. If the person you plan to sue asks within 90 days after getting your notice, you must go to examinations. That person picks the examiners, who are regulated health professionals, and pays for the examinations. You must answer the examiner's questions that relate to the examination. An examination can't be repeated without need, and it can't use a procedure that is unreasonable or dangerous. If the examiner gives a report to the person you plan to sue, that person must make sure you get a copy within 60 days after they get the report. If the person you plan to sue asks, you must give them a statutory declaration that describes what happened and your claim. If that person asks, you must also give them proof of who you are.
yourDeadline:
Serve written notice of your intention to sue on the person you will sue. You have 120 days after the incident. The court where the lawsuit could be started may allow a longer time, on a motion made before or after the 120 days run out.

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
whatHappensAfter: You can still start the lawsuit without doing these steps. But the court must take that into account when it decides costs. userQuestion: I was served with a statement of claim — what do I have to do, and by when?
whatsHappening: You have been served with a statement of claim, so you are a defendant in this action. If you want to defend, the rules set a time for you to deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A). Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. If you are a corporation, you must have a lawyer, unless the court gives leave. If you are under disability, such as a minor, or you act in a representative capacity, you must also have a lawyer.
whatToDoNext: Your defence must briefly state the key facts you rely on, but not the evidence that proves them. You must admit every fact in the claim that you do not dispute. Any fact you do not deny is treated as admitted, unless you say you have no knowledge of it. In a claim for damages, the amount is treated as in dispute unless you admit it. If your version of the facts is different, denying theirs is not enough, and you must set out your own version. You must also plead anything you rely on to defeat the claim that might surprise the plaintiff, or raise a new issue, if you left it out. You may first deliver a notice of intent to defend (Form 18B) within the time for your defence. If you do, you get 10 more days to deliver the defence. If you have a claim against the plaintiff, you may make a counterclaim. A counterclaim (Form 27A or 27B) must be in the same document as your defence, titled a statement of defence and counterclaim.
yourDeadline:
Deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A). You have 20 days after the day you were served with the statement of claim. This is the time if you were served in Ontario. If you were served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States, it is 40 days. If you were served anywhere else, it is 60 days. If you deliver a notice of intent to defend (Form 18B) in that time, you get 10 more days for the defence. Deliver means serve it on the other parties and file it with proof of service. If the claim was left at a home with an adult and a copy mailed, service takes effect on the fifth day after mailing. If it was mailed with an acknowledgment of receipt card, service takes effect on the day the sender gets the card back. If a corporation was served by mail to its last recorded address, service takes effect on the fifth day after mailing. A counterclaim against the plaintiff goes in the same document as your defence, by the same time. Your counterclaim may also name someone who is not yet a party. If so, issue it within the same time as your defence, or before you are noted in default, or later with the court's leave. Then serve and file it, with proof of service, within 30 days after it is issued. You can also do this at any time before you are noted in default, or later with the court's leave. A crossclaim against a co-defendant goes with your defence, by the same time. It can also go in at any time before you are noted in default, or later with leave. The court must give that leave unless it would prejudice the plaintiff. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court. You can still deliver a defence at any time before you are noted in default. But once the time is up, the plaintiff can have you noted in default without telling you. After that, you get no notice of further steps. If the claim is under the simplified procedure and you say it does not fit Rule 76, say so in your defence. A jury notice must be delivered before pleadings close.

You can bring in someone who is not yet a party if they are or may be liable to you for all or part of the plaintiff's claim. You can also do it for a related claim, or if they should be bound by the result. To do this, issue a third party claim (Form 29A). You have 10 days after the day you delivered your statement of defence. You can also issue it at any time before you are noted in default. Or you can issue it within 10 days after the plaintiff delivers a reply to your defence. After that, you can issue it at any time with the plaintiff's consent or the court's leave. The court must give leave unless it would prejudice the plaintiff. You must serve it within 30 days after it is issued. The two-year limitation period still applies to your claim against the third party. For a claim for contribution and indemnity, the Limitations Act, 2002 treats the day you were served with the plaintiff's claim as the day of the act or omission.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: The plaintiff may then deliver a reply within 10 days after your defence is served, or within 20 days if you made a counterclaim. If your defence is not delivered in time, the plaintiff may ask the registrar to note you in default. If you are noted in default, you are taken to admit every fact stated in the claim. Until then, you may still deliver a defence at any time.

userQuestion: How do I start my action in the Superior Court?
whatsHappening: Your action does not start until the document that starts it is issued. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, most cases cannot start more than 15 years after the act or omission they are based on. This limit does not cover claims with no limitation period, such as a case to enforce a court order or one based on a sexual assault. That 15-year period does not run during some times. One is when the person with the claim cannot sue because of their condition and has no litigation guardian. A time limit in another Act has no effect on a claim covered by the Limitations Act, 2002, with two exceptions. One is a time limit listed in the Schedule to that Act. The other is one that existed on January 1, 2004 and refers to a listed provision. Being listed does not by itself mean that the time limit applies to your claim. Section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act is listed. For libel in a newspaper or broadcast, section 5 (1) of that Act first requires written notice to the defendant of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learn of the libel. It must be served like a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. Section 6 says the case itself must start within three months after the person defamed learns of the libel. Sections 5 (1) and 6 apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario.
whatToDoNext: The usual document to start an action is a statement of claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for a mortgage action). If there is not enough time to write one, you may start with a notice of action (Form 14C) that says in short what the claim is about. You must then file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice of action is issued. After that, you need the defendant's written consent, or the court's leave obtained on notice to the defendant. File an Information for court use (Form 14F) with a Form 14A, 14B or 14C, unless you file online through one of the court portals the rule names. Rule 76 sets out a simplified procedure. It is not used for a class proceeding, a Construction Act action other than a trust claim, or an action with a jury notice. Otherwise, you must use it if your claim is only for money, real property or personal property. The money claimed plus the fair market value of the property on the day you start must also be $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. If so, your claim must say that the action is brought under Rule 76. If there are two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is checked on its own. If you sue more than one defendant, your claim against each one is checked on its own. The Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money up to a set amount, not counting interest and costs, or to recover personal property worth up to that amount. That amount is $50,000. A claim within that limit can only be started in the Superior Court with that court's leave, so you must get leave before you start it. You may ask for leave by motion without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may grant it only if it is in the interest of justice.
yourDeadline:
The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
whatHappensAfter: The registrar issues your document by dating, signing and sealing it with the court's seal and giving it a court file number. You must serve a statement of claim within six months after it is issued. If you started with a notice of action, serve both together within six months after the notice of action is issued.

userQuestion: Do I have to send a notice before I sue the government, the city, a property owner or a newspaper?
whatsHappening: You cannot sue the Ontario Crown for damages unless you serve a notice of the claim on the Crown at least 60 days before you start. A claim is different if it is about the Crown's duty as owner, occupier, possessor or controller of property. Its notice must be served no later than 10 days after the event. If a municipality did not keep a road or bridge in repair, you must give its clerk written notice within 10 days after the injury. A sidewalk can be part of a municipal road. If snow or ice on such a sidewalk hurt you, the same 10-day notice to the clerk applies. There, the municipality is liable only for gross negligence. If snow or ice on someone's premises hurt you, you must give written notice to the occupier or their snow contractor. You have 60 days after the injury. For a libel in a newspaper or broadcast from Ontario, you must give the defendant written notice. You have six weeks after you learn of the libel.
whatToDoNext: Leave the notice to the Crown with an employee at the Crown Law Office (Civil Law) of the Ministry of the Attorney General. The notice to a municipality must give the date, time and place. Serve it on the clerk or send it by registered mail. If two or more municipalities share the duty to repair the road or bridge, give notice to the clerk of each. In Toronto, the City of Toronto Act, 2006 sets the same 10-day notice, given to the city clerk. For snow or ice, the notice must also give the date, time and place. It must be personally served on, or sent by registered mail to, the occupier or the contractor. For a libel, the notice must say what you complain of. Serve it like a statement of claim, or give it to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. You must then start the libel action within three months after you learned of the libel. This shorter time counts because the Schedule to the Limitations Act, 2002 lists section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act.
yourDeadline:
If you are claiming damages from the Ontario Crown, serve a notice of claim on the Crown. Do this at least 60 days before the day you start the action. A claim against the Crown or a Crown officer or employee for misfeasance in public office or bad faith needs the court's leave. Until leave is given, it is stayed. Earlier is fine. Serve the notice as section 15 of the Act requires. That means leaving a copy with an employee at the Crown Law Office (Civil Law) of the Ministry of the Attorney General. The notice must give enough detail to identify the event the claim came from. The Attorney General may ask for more details to look into the claim. The 60 days count back from the day the action starts. So serving later, even because of a Sunday or holiday, leaves fewer than 60 days. An action started without the notice has no effect (it is a nullity). A claim about a duty that comes with owning, occupying, possessing or controlling property is different. Its notice must be served no later than 10 days after the event. The notice requirement does not apply to a counterclaim, crossclaim or set-off. Sometimes the notice is served before the limitation period ends, but the 60 days end after it. Then the limitation period is extended to the end of the seventh day after the 60 days.

If a municipality did not keep a highway (road) or bridge in repair and you claim damages, give written notice of the claim to the municipal clerk. You have 10 days after the day of the injury. This covers all damages a person suffers because of the failure to repair. The same section covers injury from snow or ice on a municipal sidewalk. There, the municipality is liable only for gross negligence. If you were hurt on a municipal sidewalk, this 10-day notice to the clerk may be the one that applies, not the 60-day notice to an occupier. The notice must give the date, time and place. Serve it on the clerk, or send it by registered mail. If two or more municipalities share the duty to repair the road or bridge, notify the clerk of each. In Toronto, the City of Toronto Act, 2006 sets the same 10 days, with notice to the city clerk. Missing the notice is not a bar if the injured person died from the injury. It is also not a bar if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and no prejudice to the municipality.

If you were hurt by snow or ice on someone's premises, give written notice of the claim to an occupier or to their snow-removal contractor. You have 60 days after the day of the injury. The notice must give the date, time and place. Serve it in person or send it by registered mail. Missing the notice is not a bar if the injured person died from the injury. It is also not a bar if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and no prejudice to the defendant.

If you are suing over a libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast, give the defendant written notice that specifies the matter you complain of. You have 42 days after the day the libel came to your knowledge. The Act says six weeks, which is 42 days. Serve the notice the same way as a statement of claim, or give it to an adult at the defendant's chief office. This applies only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario, and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario. A newspaper cannot rely on it unless it prints its owner's and publisher's names and its address of publication. These must appear at the head of the editorials or on the front page. For a broadcast, you may ask the station by registered letter for the owner's or operator's name and address. If the station does not give them within ten days after it gets your letter, this does not apply against that owner or operator.

If you are suing over a libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast, start the action. You have 3 months after the day the libel came to your knowledge. This shorter time replaces the general two years, because the Limitations Act lists it in its schedule. It applies only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario, and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario. A newspaper cannot rely on it unless it prints its owner's and publisher's names and its address of publication. These must appear at the head of the editorials or on the front page. For a broadcast, you may ask the station by registered letter for the owner's or operator's name and address. If the station does not give them within ten days after it gets your letter, this does not apply against that owner or operator.

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
whatHappensAfter: An action against the Crown started without the notice is a nullity for that claim. Missing the notice to a municipality is not a bar if the injured person died from the injury. It is also not a bar if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and no prejudice to the municipality in its defence. For snow or ice on someone's premises, failure to give notice is not a bar if the injured person died from the injury. It is also not a bar if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and no prejudice to the defendant in its defence. Apart from these notices, a case generally cannot be started more than two years after the day the claim was discovered. Also, a case can't start more than 15 years after the act or omission it is based on, with some exceptions.

userQuestion: There is a motion in my case — what do I have to file, and when?
whatsHappening: A motion is made by a notice of motion (Form 37A), unless the rules or the situation make one unnecessary. The notice must state the exact order asked for, the grounds, and the documents that will be used as evidence. When a motion is made on notice, the notice of motion must be served at least seven days before the hearing. The notice of motion must also be filed with proof of service at least seven days before the hearing, in the court office where the motion will be heard. The moving party may propose in the notice that the motion be heard in writing. If so, the motion must be made on at least 14 days notice.
whatToDoNext: If you are bringing the motion, you must serve a motion record on every other party, unless the court orders otherwise. File it with proof of service at least seven days before the hearing. The motion record has a table of contents, the notice of motion, and all affidavits and other material served for the motion. It also has a list of all relevant transcripts of evidence, and any other material in the court file needed for the hearing. If you are bringing a motion on notice, you must also confer or try to confer with the other party. Then, no later than 2 p.m. five days before the hearing date, give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B). Email it to the court office or leave it there, and email a copy to the other party. If no confirmation is given, the motion is not heard and is treated as abandoned, unless the court orders otherwise. If you propose a hearing in writing, serve a motion record, a draft order and a factum for a motion in writing with the notice of motion. File them right away, with proof of service. In a simplified procedure action, you must serve a motion form (Form 76B) as rule 37.07 requires. For a motion on notice, that means at least seven days before the hearing. You must also submit the form to the court before the motion is brought and heard. There, the motion may be made with or without supporting material or a motion record, depending on what the situation needs. If you are responding and think the motion record is incomplete, you may serve and file your own responding party's motion record, with proof of service. Do this at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and any material you will use that is not in the moving party's record. If you are responding to a motion proposed to be heard in writing, you must serve and file a response, with proof of service. Do this within 10 days after you are served with the moving party's material. Your response can be a consent to the motion, or a notice that you do not oppose it. It can be your motion record, a notice that you agree to a hearing in writing, and a factum for a motion in writing. Or it can be a notice that you intend to make oral argument, with any material you will rely on. Either party may serve a factum on every other party. If you do, you must also file it with proof of service. Do this at least seven days before the hearing if you brought the motion. If you are responding, do it at least four days before the hearing.
yourDeadline:
If you are bringing the motion, serve the notice of motion and motion record on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. Your factum, if you have one, is due by the same day. userQuestion: I was served with family court papers — what do I have to do, and by when?
whatsHappening: An application, or a claim in another party's answer, has been made against you in a family case. You must serve an answer on every other party and file it. When the application was filed, the clerk had to set a court date, except in some cases. In the Ontario Court of Justice, and in a fast track case in the Family Court, the clerk acts on or before the first court date. If no answer to the application has been filed, the clerk sends the case to a judge to decide on affidavit evidence, or sets a case conference if the applicant asks.
whatToDoNext: The answer is Form 10. The other forms rule 10 (1) lists are for child protection cases and other cases under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. Your answer may include a claim against the applicant, or against another person, who then also becomes a respondent. The application may claim support, property, or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents. If it does, you must serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1) within the time for your answer, even if you do not serve an answer. If your own answer makes one of those claims, you must serve and file a financial statement with your answer. You do not need one for your claim if your only support claim is for child support in the table amount. That exception does not apply if your answer also has a property claim or a claim for the matrimonial home. You also do not need one if your only claim is about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. Use Form 13 for a support claim with no property claim and no claim for the matrimonial home. Use Form 13.1 if there is a property claim or a claim for the matrimonial home, with or without a support claim. If your answer claims decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child, it must come with the documents rule 35.1 lists. Some cases need the mandatory information program. In those cases, you may not take any other step until your certificate of attendance is filed. You may still serve and file an answer, and make an appointment for a case conference.
yourDeadline:
Serve an answer on every other party and file it. You have 30 days after the day of being served with the application. If you were served outside Canada and the United States, you have 60 days. If another party’s answer added you as a respondent, you have 14 days. That becomes 30 days if you were served outside Canada and the United States. Other times apply to an application to dispense with a parent’s consent before adoption placement. Service rules decide when your time starts. Papers left at your home with an adult, with a copy mailed, count as served on the fifth day after mailing. Papers left with you after 4 p.m. count as served the next day. If that day is one when court offices are closed, service counts on the next open day. For mail with an acknowledgment card, the rules set no separate start day. The general rule for mail is the fifth day after mailing. That service counts only once the card you signed is filed. If the application claims support, property or the matrimonial home against you, your financial statement is due in the same time. For a support claim with no property claim, serve the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) with it. If your answer claims decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, add the papers rule 35.1 requires. Your answer may make its own claim about parenting, property or support. If the clerk then issues an automatic order, serve it on every other party promptly, and no later than 7 days after it is issued. If you miss the time, then unless the court orders otherwise, you lose the right to notice of further steps. Any order must still be served on you. You cannot take part in the case. The court may decide the case without you. A date may be set for an uncontested trial. The court office will refuse a late answer. It will take one only if the other parties agree in writing or the court gives more time. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

If the application or your answer has a property claim, serve the other party with the property papers the rule lists. You have 30 days after the day your financial statement was due, which is the last day for your answer. For a claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, the rule lists the papers. One example is the statement closest to the valuation date for each bank or other account. For any other property claim, serve the information needed to support the claim. If there is also a support claim, serve the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) with it. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with the papers. The court can order otherwise. If the property claim is your own claim in your answer, your financial statement is due with the answer. So if you serve your answer early, count the 30 days from that day.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. The applicant books your appointment and serves notice of it with the application. The 45 days run from the day the application was filed, not the day you were served. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take other steps. You can still serve and file an answer. You can also book a case conference.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If you do not serve and file an answer, then unless a court orders otherwise, you lose the right to notice of further steps, except service of an order. You cannot take part in the case, the court may deal with it without you, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial. If your answer makes a claim, a party served with it may serve and file a reply (Form 10A) within 10 days after being served with it.

userQuestion: I filed my application — how do I get it to the other parent or my ex?
whatsHappening: You have filed your application, but it has not been served on the respondent yet. When an application is filed, the clerk must seal it with the court seal. The clerk must also set a court date, except in two kinds of cases. In the Family Court, a claim for divorce, a property claim or a family arbitration claim makes the case a standard track case. In a standard track case, no court date is set when the application is filed. In the Superior Court of Justice outside the Family Court, no court date is set when the application is filed either. In both kinds of cases, the clerk must schedule a case conference if any party asks.
whatToDoNext: You must serve the application on every other party right away. You must use special service, unless the party is one of those listed in r. 8 (6). Someone other than you must carry out the special service, unless the court orders otherwise, and that person must be at least 18 years old. The rule that someone other than you must serve it also does not apply if you or the person served is one of the officials or agencies in r. 8 (6) (c). The person serving must always be at least 18. One way to do special service is to leave a copy with the person to be served. Another way is to leave a copy at their home, in an envelope addressed to them, with an adult who appears to live there. Then, on the same day or the next, another copy is mailed to them at that address. A copy can also be mailed to the person with a prepaid return postcard (Form 6). Both must go in an envelope addressed to the person that has the sender's return address. That way is valid only once the postcard, signed by the person, is filed in the continuing record. You must also prepare the continuing record, serve it on all other parties, and file it with proof that it was served.
yourDeadline:
Serve the application on every other party right away, by special service. The rule sets no number of days. It says the application must be served immediately. Someone other than you must do the special service, unless the court orders otherwise. Serve the continuing record on all other parties too. File it with proof of service. Some papers must go with the application. In a case about parenting, net family property, the matrimonial home or support, include the automatic order (Form 8.0.1). Include your financial statement if one is required. For a support claim with no property claim, also include the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) and a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). The clerk will not accept a financial statement for a support claim without proof of your income. You need proof of your current income and of your income for the past three years. For a claim about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, include the papers rule 35.1 requires. If you are not the child's parent and ask for decision-making responsibility, attach a police records check to Form 35.1. If you only have proof that you asked for the check, serve and file the check within 10 days after you get it. If the application is not served by its court date, the clerk must set a new date if you ask. You then serve it right away.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. You book your own appointment and the respondent’s. Serve notice of the respondent’s appointment with the application. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take another step in the case. The one exception is booking a case conference. The court can order otherwise on a motion.

If your application makes a property claim, serve the respondent with the property papers the rule lists. You have 30 days after the day your financial statement was due, which is the day you served the application. For a claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, the rule lists the papers. One example is the statement closest to the valuation date for each bank or other account. For any other property claim, serve the information needed to support the claim. If there is also a support claim, serve the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) with it. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with the papers. The court can order otherwise.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If the application is not served by the court date, the clerk must set a new court date for that respondent if you ask. You then change the application to match and serve it on that respondent right away. Once served, the respondent must serve an answer on every other party and file it within 30 days. If the application is served outside Canada or the United States, that time is 60 days.

In a standard track case, (a) the clerk shall not set a court date when the application is filed; (b) a case management judge shall be assigned when a case conference or a motion is scheduled, whichever comes first; and (c) the clerk shall schedule a case conference on any party’s request.

If an application is not served on a respondent on or before the court date, at the applicant’s request the clerk shall set a new court date for that respondent and the applicant shall make the necessary change to the application and serve it immediately on that respondent.

userQuestion: I have a case conference coming up — what do I have to file, and when?
whatsHappening: One purpose of a case conference is to explore settling the case. Other purposes include finding which issues are in dispute and which are not, and looking at ways to resolve them. It is also meant to make sure the relevant evidence is shared, including financial information needed for any support or property issue. It can set the date for the next step in the case. No motion may be served or heard until a conference on the main issues is done. That does not apply if the court finds there is urgency or hardship. It also does not apply if the court finds a case conference is not needed for another reason in the interest of justice. Nor does it apply to certain motions listed in rule 14 (6). These include any motion in a child protection case. They also include a motion made without notice, made on consent, or unopposed. Another is a motion limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters.
whatToDoNext: If you are the one who asked for the case conference, you must serve and file a case conference notice (Form 17). Each party must serve and file a case conference brief (Form 17A or 17B). Each party must also give the clerk a confirmation of conference (Form 17F). Before that, give a copy to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other way, except in a child protection case. You can give it to the clerk by delivering it to the court office, by email, or through the Justice Services Online website or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. Unless the court orders otherwise, the conference will not be held if the clerk does not get it by 2 p.m. three days before the conference date. Rule 13 (3.1), (3.3), (3.4) and (5.0.1) list extra financial disclosure documents for a support claim, a property claim, and a motion to change support. If you had to serve those documents, you must serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with them and file the certificate. The parties must come to the conference, unless the court orders otherwise. A party who has a licensed representative must also bring that representative, with full knowledge of and authority in the case.
yourDeadline:
If you served the case conference notice (Form 17), serve and file your case conference brief. If no one asked for the conference, this time is for the applicant or the party who made the motion. Do this at least 6 days before the date of the case conference. Your last financial statement may be more than 60 days old by the conference. If so, update it by this same day. Serve and file an affidavit saying nothing has changed, an affidavit with the changes, or a new statement. If there is a support claim, give the other party the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) before the case conference, unless you already served them. Before the conference, talk or write to every other party, or make your best effort to. Discuss requests for financial disclosure and settling the issues for now. You do not have to if a court order forbids it. You also do not have to if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party with no licensed representative. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the other party, serve and file your case conference brief. Do this at least 4 days before the date of the case conference. The extra steps listed above apply to you too. Where they say "by the same day", your day is this 4-day one. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Give a copy of the confirmation of conference (Form 17F) to every other party. Then give it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 3 days before the date of the case conference. The parties cannot change this time by agreement. Unless the court orders otherwise, the conference will not go ahead without it.

If you are the applicant or the party who made the motion, and you had to serve financial disclosure, file your certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). Do this at least 6 days before the date of the case conference. You also serve the certificate with the disclosure papers. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the other party and had to serve financial disclosure, file your certificate (Form 13A). Do this at least 4 days before the date of the case conference. You also serve the certificate with the disclosure papers. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

File your information program certificate of attendance as soon as you can, and no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 2 days before the date of the case conference. This applies only if the program applies to the case. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: At the conference, the judge may, if it is right to do so, order document disclosure or questioning, set times for steps in the case, or give directions for the next steps. If notice has been served, the judge may also make a final order or a temporary order. An agreement reached at a conference does not take effect until the parties sign it and it is witnessed, and in some cases the court must approve it. A case cannot be set for trial unless a settlement conference has been held or a judge has ordered it.

userQuestion: The other side's financial disclosure is incomplete — how do I get the rest?
whatsHappening: You think the other party's financial papers do not give enough information to fully understand their finances. A party who finds that a financial disclosure paper they served is wrong, incomplete or out of date must serve a new or corrected one right away. They must also file it, if that applies. A party who finds they did not serve one of the extra disclosure documents rule 13 requires must serve it as soon as they find out.
whatToDoNext: First, you must ask the other party in writing for the extra information you need. If any of it is not given within seven days of your request, the court may order them to give it or to serve and file a new financial statement. The court can do this on a motion, or at a case or settlement conference. When you ask for this order, you must list in your motion or conference brief the information you asked for but did not get. No motion may be served or heard until a conference on the main issues is done. That does not apply if the court finds there is urgency or hardship. It also does not apply if the court finds a case conference is not needed for another reason in the interest of justice. It also does not apply to certain motions listed in rule 14 (6). These include any motion in a child protection case. They also include a motion made without notice, made on consent, or unopposed. Another is a motion limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters. A motion form (Form 14B) may be used to ask for this order. A party may be questioned on their financial statement under rule 20, but only after a written request for information has been made. Outside a child protection case, questioning needs the other party's consent or a court order. The court can order it on a motion only if three things are true. It would be unfair to go on without it. The information is not easy to get another way. And it will not cause unacceptable delay or undue expense. In a child protection case, a party is entitled to question the other party without an order. To do so, they must serve the other party with a summons to witness (Form 23) by special service. This does not apply to an application for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. To question, you must first have served and filed any answer, financial statement or net family property statement the rules require. You must also promise in writing not to serve or file more material for the next step, except in reply to what you learn.
yourDeadline:
The other party's time to give the additional financial information you asked for in writing. They have 7 days after the day of the written request. If it is not given in that time, the court can order it. It can do so on a motion or at a case or settlement conference. In your motion or conference brief, say what you asked for and did not get.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: If a party has not served or filed a document the financial disclosure rule requires, the court may order them to do it, on a motion. If the court makes that order, it must also order that party to pay costs. One purpose of a case conference is to make sure financial information needed for any support or property issue is shared.

userQuestion: Can I sue over this in the Superior Court, and am I still in time?
whatsHappening: Nothing has been filed yet. You are working out whether the Superior Court of Justice is the place for your dispute, and whether you are still in time. Which court can hear a claim for money depends on the amount claimed, not counting interest and costs. For a claim to get back personal property, it depends on the value of the property. The most the Small Claims Court can hear is a claim for $50,000.
whatToDoNext: A case that is within the Small Claims Court's limits must not be started in the Superior Court of Justice unless the Superior Court gives leave. The court may give that leave only if it is in the interest of justice. You may ask for this leave without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. Leave is not needed for a counterclaim, a crossclaim, or a third or later party claim, if the main case was started in the Superior Court. In the Superior Court, a set of steps called the simplified procedure must be used if two things are true. First, your claim is only for money, real property or personal property, or some of these. Second, the total is $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. The total is the money claimed plus the fair market value of any property on the day the case starts. If there are two or more plaintiffs or defendants, each claim is considered separately. The simplified procedure does not apply to some cases, such as cases under the Class Proceedings Act, 1992. It also stops applying if a party delivers a jury notice. A party may do that only if the case involves a claim arising from slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.
yourDeadline:
The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
whatHappensAfter: Unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise, a case cannot be started more than two years after the day the claim was discovered. Some proceedings fall outside the Limitations Act, 2002. One example is a proceeding the Real Property Limitations Act applies to. Even if the two years have not run out, no case can be started more than 15 years after the day the act or omission it is based on took place. Some claims have no time limit at all, such as a claim based on a sexual assault. That 15-year period does not run during some times, including these two. One is while you are a minor and have no litigation guardian. The other is while a physical, mental or psychological condition makes you unable to start a case, and you have no litigation guardian. Some time limits in other Acts are listed in the Schedule to the Limitations Act, 2002. One is section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act. It covers a case for libel in a newspaper or broadcast. That case must be started within three months after the person defamed learned of the libel. First, you must give the defendant written notice of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learned of the libel. The notice must be served the same way as a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. These two time limits apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario. The Libel and Slander Act also sets conditions a newspaper or broadcaster must meet to rely on them.

citations.quote: The Small Claims Court, (a) has jurisdiction in any action for the payment of money where the amount claimed does not exceed the prescribed amount exclusive of interest and costs; and (b) has jurisdiction in any action for the recovery of possession of personal property where the value of the property does not exceed the prescribed amount.
The maximum amount of a claim in the Small Claims Court is $50,000.

An action that is within the Small Claims Court's jurisdiction shall not, despite subsection 11 (2), be commenced in the Superior Court of Justice except with leave of the Superior Court of Justice as provided in the rules of court.
Subsection (1.1) does not apply with respect to a counterclaim, crossclaim or third or subsequent party claim, where the main action was commenced in the Superior Court of Justice.

A motion under subsection 23 (1.1) of the Courts of Justice Act for leave to commence an action in the Superior Court of Justice that is within the Small Claims Court's jurisdiction may be made without notice, unless the court orders otherwise.
The court may grant leave under subsection 23 (1.1) of the Courts of Justice Act only if it is in the interest of justice.
The simplified procedure set out in this Rule does not apply to, (a) actions under the Class Proceedings Act, 1992;

The procedure set out in this Rule shall be used in an action if the following conditions are satisfied: 1. The plaintiff's claim is exclusively for one or more of the following: i. Money. ii. Real property. iii. Personal property. 2. The total of the following amounts is $200,000 or less exclusive of interest and costs: i. The amount of money claimed, if any. ii. The fair market value of any real property and of any personal property, as at the date the action is commenced.
If there are two or more plaintiffs, the procedure set out in this Rule shall be used if each plaintiff's claim, considered separately, meets the requirements of subrule (1).
If there are two or more defendants, the procedure set out in this Rule shall be used if the plaintiff's claim against each defendant, considered separately, meets the requirements of subrule (1).
An action that is proceeding under this Rule shall not be tried with a jury and, subject to subrule (2), no party to the action may deliver a jury notice under rule 47.01.

A party to an action that is proceeding under this Rule may deliver a jury notice under rule 47.01 if the action involves a claim for relief arising from one of the following: 1. Slander. 2. Libel. 3. Malicious arrest. 4. Malicious prosecution. 5. False imprisonment.
If a jury notice is delivered in accordance with subrule (2), the action may no longer proceed under this Rule
Unless this Act provides otherwise, a proceeding shall not be commenced in respect of a claim after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered.
This Act applies to claims pursued in court proceedings other than, (a) proceedings to which the Real Property Limitations Act applies;

Even if the limitation period established by any other section of this Act in respect of a claim has not expired, no proceeding shall be commenced in respect of the claim after the expiry of a limitation period established by this section.
No proceeding shall be commenced in respect of any claim after the 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission on which the claim is based took place.

The limitation period established by subsection (2) does not run during any time in which, (a) the person with the claim, (i) is incapable of commencing a proceeding in respect of the claim because of his or her physical, mental or psychological condition, and (ii) is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim; (b) the person with the claim is a minor and is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim; or (c) the person against whom the claim is made, (i) wilfully conceals from the person with the claim the fact that injury, loss or damage has occurred, that it was caused by or contributed to by an act or omission or that the act or omission was that of the person against whom the claim is made, or (ii) wilfully misleads the person with the claim as to the appropriateness of a proceeding as a means of remedying the injury, loss or damage.
There is no limitation period in respect of, ... (h) a proceeding based on a sexual assault;

No action for libel in a newspaper or in a broadcast lies unless the plaintiff has, within six weeks after the alleged libel has come to the plaintiff's knowledge, given to the defendant notice in writing, specifying the matter complained of, which shall be served in the same manner as a statement of claim or by delivering it to a grown-up person at the chief office of the defendant.

userQuestion: This happened years ago — is it too late to sue?
whatsHappening: More than two years seem to have passed since the events. But the day the claim was discovered has not been worked out yet. Unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise, you have two years from the day the claim was discovered to start a case. Some proceedings fall outside the Limitations Act, 2002. One example is a proceeding the Real Property Limitations Act applies to. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you first knew four things. First, that the injury, loss or damage happened. Second, that an act or omission caused it or helped cause it. Third, that it was the act or omission of the person you would sue. Fourth, that given the kind of loss, a court case would be a fitting way to try to fix it. The second is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities, in your circumstances, ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless it is proved otherwise. Some claims are about a demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004. For those, the loss happens on the first day the obligation is not performed after a demand is made.
whatToDoNext: The two years do not run while you are a minor and have no litigation guardian for the claim. They also do not run while a physical, mental or psychological condition makes you unable to start a case, and you have no litigation guardian for the claim. You are presumed to have been able to start a case at all times, unless it is proved otherwise. If a pause for such a condition ends with less than six months left, the time is extended to six months after the day it ends. Time also stops while you and the other person have agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim or help you resolve it. It starts again when the claim is resolved, when that process ends, or when one of you ends or withdraws from the agreement. This pause covers both the two years and the 15 years described below. The other person, or their agent, may have admitted liability in writing and signed it. For some claims, the act or omission is then treated as taking place on the day of that admission. These include a claim for a fixed sum of money or to get back personal property. This counts only if the admission was made before the time ran out. It must also have been made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other person or their agent has the same effect.
yourDeadline:
The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel. The two years do not run while the person with the claim is a minor and has no litigation guardian. They also do not run while a physical, mental or psychological condition keeps the person from starting a case, and they have no litigation guardian. A person is presumed able to start a case unless shown otherwise. If that condition ends with less than six months left, the time runs to six months after it ends. The 15 years also do not run while the other side wilfully hides from you that the loss happened, that an act or omission caused it, or that it was theirs. Nor do they run while the other side wilfully misleads you about whether a court case is a proper way to fix it. You must prove this. The two years and the 15 years also stop while the parties have agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim or help resolve it. The other side may admit in writing, and sign, that they owe a fixed sum of money. The same goes for an admission that they must return personal property. It also goes for enforcing a charge on personal property, or relief from that. Then the act or omission is treated as happening on the day of that admission. This counts only if it was made before the time ran out. It must be made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other side or their agent works the same way as a written, signed admission. For a debt payable on demand, the loss happens on the first day it is not paid after a demand for payment.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
whatHappensAfter: Separately, no case can be started more than 15 years after the day of the act or omission, even if the two years have not run out. For the 15 years, an act or omission that goes on over time counts from the day it stops. A series of acts or omissions about the same obligation counts from the day of the last one. For a demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004, it counts from the first day the obligation is not performed after a demand. Some claims have no time limit at all, such as a claim based on a sexual assault. The 15 years do not run while you are a minor, or unable to start a case because of a physical, mental or psychological condition, and have no litigation guardian. They also do not run while the other person wilfully hides from you that the loss happened, that an act or omission caused it, or that it was theirs. Nor do they run while the other person wilfully misleads you about whether a court case is a fitting way to fix the loss. The burden of proving that one of these 15-year pauses applies is on you. Some time limits in other Acts are listed in the Schedule to the Limitations Act, 2002. One is section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act. It covers a case for libel in a newspaper or broadcast. That case must be started within three months after the person defamed learned of the libel. First, you must give the defendant written notice of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learned of the libel. The notice must be served the same way as a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. These two time limits apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario. The Libel and Slander Act also sets conditions a newspaper or broadcaster must meet to rely on them.

citations.quote: This Act applies to claims pursued in court proceedings other than, (a) proceedings to which the Real Property Limitations Act applies;
Unless this Act provides otherwise, a proceeding shall not be commenced in respect of a claim after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered.

A claim is discovered on the earlier of, (a) the day on which the person with the claim first knew, (i) that the injury, loss or damage had occurred, (ii) that the injury, loss or damage was caused by or contributed to by an act or omission, (iii) that the act or omission was that of the person against whom the claim is made, and (iv) that, having regard to the nature of the injury, loss or damage, a proceeding would be an appropriate means to seek to remedy it; and (b) the day on which a reasonable person with the abilities and in the circumstances of the person with the claim first ought to have known of the matters referred to in clause (a).

For the purposes of subclause (1) (a) (i), the day on which injury, loss or damage occurs in relation to a demand obligation is the first day on which there is a failure to perform the obligation, once a demand for the performance is made.
Subsection (3) applies in respect of every demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004.

For the purposes of this section, the day an act or omission on which a claim is based takes place is, (a) in the case of a continuous act or omission, the day on which the act or omission ceases; (b) in the case of a series of acts or omissions in respect of the same obligation, the day on which the last act or omission in the series occurs; (c) in the case of an act or omission in respect of a demand obligation, the first day on which there is a failure to perform the obligation, once a demand for the performance is made.
Clause (6) (c) applies in respect of every demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004.

A person with a claim shall be presumed to have known of the matters referred to in clause (1) (a) on the day the act or omission on which the claim is based took place, unless the contrary is proved.

The limitation period established by section 4 does not run during any time in which the person with the claim, (a) is a minor; and (b) is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim.

The limitation period established by section 4 does not run during any time in which the person with the claim, (a) is incapable of commencing a proceeding in respect of the claim because of his or her physical, mental or psychological condition; and (b) is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim.
A person shall be presumed to have been capable of commencing a proceeding in respect of a claim at all times unless the contrary is proved.

If the running of a limitation period is postponed or suspended under this section and the period has less than six months to run when the postponement or suspension ends, the period is extended to include the day that is six months after the day on which the postponement or suspension ends.

If a person with a claim and a person against whom the claim is made have agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim or assist them in resolving it, the limitation periods established by sections 4 and 15 do not run from the date the agreement is made until, (a) the date the claim is resolved; (b) the date the attempted resolution process is terminated; or (c) the date a party terminates or withdraws from the agreement.

If a person acknowledges liability in respect of a claim for payment of a liquidated sum, the recovery of personal property, the enforcement of a charge on personal property or relief from enforcement of a charge on personal property, the act or omission on which the claim is based shall be deemed to have taken place on the day on which the acknowledgment was made.

This section does not apply unless the acknowledgment is made to the person with the claim, the person's agent or an official receiver or trustee acting under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada) before the expiry of the limitation period applicable to the claim.
Subsections (1), (2), (3), (6) and (7) do not apply unless the acknowledgment is in writing and signed by the person making it or the person's agent.

In the case of a claim for payment of a liquidated sum, part payment of the sum by the person against whom the claim is made or by the person's agent has the same effect as the acknowledgment referred to in subsection (10).

Even if the limitation period established by any other section of this Act in respect of a claim has not expired, no proceeding shall be commenced in respect of the claim after the expiry of a limitation period established by this section.
No proceeding shall be commenced in respect of any claim after the 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission on which the claim is based took place.

The limitation period established by subsection (2) does not run during any time in which, (a) the person with the claim, (i) is incapable of commencing a proceeding in respect of the claim because of his or her physical, mental or psychological condition, and (ii) is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim; (b) the person with the claim is a minor and is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim; or (c) the person against whom the claim is made, (i) wilfully conceals from the person with the claim the fact that injury, loss or damage has occurred, that it was caused by or contributed to by an act or omission or that the act or omission was that of the person against whom the claim is made, or (ii) wilfully misleads the person with the claim as to the appropriateness of a proceeding as a means of remedying the injury, loss or damage.
The burden of proving that subsection (4) applies is on the person with the claim.
There is no limitation period in respect of, ... (h) a proceeding based on a sexual assault;
A limitation period set out in or under another Act that applies to a claim to which this Act applies is of no effect unless, (a) the provision establishing it is listed in the Schedule to this Act;
LIBEL AND SLANDER ACT |SECTION 6 |

No action for libel in a newspaper or in a broadcast lies unless the plaintiff has, within six weeks after the alleged libel has come to the plaintiff's knowledge, given to the defendant notice in writing, specifying the matter complained of, which shall be served in the same manner as a statement of claim or by delivering it to a grown-up person at the chief office of the defendant.
An action for a libel in a newspaper or in a broadcast shall be commenced within three months after the libel has come to the knowledge of the person defamed
Subsection 5 (1) and section 6 apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario.
