userQuestion: I need a temporary order before the case is over — how do I bring a motion?
whatsHappening: You may make a motion if you want a temporary order for a claim made in an application. You may also make one to get directions on how to carry on the case, or to change a temporary order. A motion may be made by a party to the case or by a person with an interest in the case. In most cases, no motion papers may be served and no motion may be heard until a conference on the main issues in the case is done. That wait does not apply if the court finds there is urgency or hardship. It also does not apply if the court finds a case conference is not needed for another reason in the interest of justice. Nor does it apply to the motions listed in rule 14 (6). These include a motion made without notice, made on consent, or unopposed, or one limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters. They also include a motion for summary judgment and any motion in a child protection case.
whatToDoNext: A motion needs a notice of motion (Form 14) and an affidavit (Form 14A), and it may be supported by more evidence. If your motion is only about procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters, you may use a motion form (Form 14B) instead. An affidavit must, as much as possible, contain only what the person signing it knows personally. Unless the court orders otherwise, you must serve all the evidence in support of the motion with the notice of motion. For a motion with notice, you must serve these papers on all other parties no later than six days before the motion date. You must file them as soon as possible after you serve them, but no later than four days before the motion date. You must also talk or write to every other party about the issues in dispute in the motion, or make your best efforts to. You do not have to if a court order forbids it, or if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party who has no licensed representative. Before you give the clerk the confirmation of motion (Form 14C), you must give a copy to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other method. That copy step does not apply in child protection cases, except applications for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. You must give the clerk the confirmation of motion no later than 2 p.m. three days before the motion date. You can deliver it to the court office, email it to the court office, or submit it through the Justice Services Online website or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. Unless the court orders otherwise, the motion will not be heard if the clerk does not get the confirmation on time. A motion may be made without notice in the cases rule 14 (12) lists. These include when the nature or circumstances of the motion make notice unnecessary or not reasonably possible. For a motion without notice, you must file the papers on or before the motion date, unless the court orders otherwise.
yourDeadline:
Serve your notice of motion and affidavit (or your motion form) on all other parties. Do this at least 6 days before the date the motion will be heard. In most cases, you cannot serve a motion or have it heard until a conference on the main issues is done. The court can allow it sooner for urgency, hardship or another reason in the interest of justice. The wait does not apply to the motions the rule lists. Examples are motions without notice, on consent, unopposed or procedural (Form 14B). It also does not apply to a motion for summary judgment, or to change an order for fraud, mistake or lack of notice. Before the motion, talk or write to every other party about the issues, or make your best effort to. You do not have to if a court order forbids it. You also do not have to if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party with no licensed representative. Where the information program applies, you cannot bring a motion until your certificate is filed. The court can order otherwise, for example for urgency or hardship. Your last financial statement may be more than 30 days old when the motion is heard. If so, update it by this same day with an affidavit or a new statement. If the motion claims support, property or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home, serve and file a financial statement with it. Do the same if it asks to change temporary support. For a motion without notice, file the papers on or before the motion date. If the court then makes an order, serve it right away on every party affected. Serve all the motion papers with it, unless the court orders otherwise. The order sets a return date within 14 days, or on a date the court chooses. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

File your motion papers. File them as soon as you can after you serve them. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Give a copy of the confirmation of motion (Form 14C) to every other party. Then give it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 3 days before the date the motion will be heard. The parties cannot change this time by agreement. Unless the court orders otherwise, the motion will not be heard without it. If you used a notice of motion and got a response, any reply is due by this same time. If you used a motion form (Form 14B), you cannot reply to a response.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: A response to a notice of motion must be served and filed no later than four days before the motion date. If you used a notice of motion and are served with a response, you may serve and file a reply no later than 2 p.m. three days before the motion date. If you used a motion form (Form 14B), you may not serve or file a reply. An order made on a motion without notice must require the matter to come back to the court within 14 days or on a date the court chooses, and to the same judge if possible.

userQuestion: I was served with a motion — how do I respond, and by when?

whatToDoNext: If you were served with a notice of motion, you must serve and file your response no later than four days before the motion date. Unless the court orders otherwise, you must serve all your evidence in response to the motion. With the court's permission, it may also be given by oral evidence. An affidavit must, as much as possible, contain only what the person signing it knows personally. It may also contain what the person learned from someone else, but only if it names that source and says the person signing believes it is true. For a contempt motion under rule 31, rule 14 (19) adds one more condition for this kind of information.
yourDeadline:
If you were served with a notice of motion (Form 14), serve and file your response. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. Your last financial statement may be more than 30 days old when the motion is heard. If so, update it by this same day with an affidavit or a new statement. The motion may claim support, property or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home against you. If so, serve and file your financial statement by this same day, even if you do not respond. userQuestion: Things have changed since the final order — how do I ask the court to change it?
whatsHappening: You want the court to change a final order. The same steps apply to a support agreement filed under section 35 of the Family Law Act. They also apply to a family arbitration award filed under section 59.9 of that Act. They do not apply to an order under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. The one exception is a final order under section 102 of that Act. You can ask for the change only by a motion to change under rule 15, if that rule allows it. There are two exceptions. First, rule 25 (19) lets the court change an order on a motion in some cases. Examples are an order made by fraud, one with a mistake, or one made without notice. Second, you may want to make related claims that fall outside rule 15 as well. Then you may file an application to deal with the change and those claims together. A motion to change starts where rule 5 says a new case would start. The places rule 5 names include the town or city where a party lives. Is the case about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child? Then it starts where the child usually lives. The one exception is set out in section 22 of the Children's Law Reform Act.
whatToDoNext: Unless the parties and any assignee all agree to the change, you must serve and file a motion to change (Form 15). Add all required attachments. Attach a copy of any order or agreement that deals with decision-making responsibility, parenting time, contact or support. Does your motion make a claim about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child? Then you must also include the papers rule 35.1 requires. With the motion, you must serve the other party a blank response (Form 15B). You must also serve a blank consent motion to change (Form 15C). These papers must be served by special service, and not by regular service. But you may use regular service on the people listed in rule 8 (6). They include foster parents, band or First Nations, Inuit or Métis community representatives, and certain officials and agencies. Someone other than you must carry out special service of the motion to change. That does not apply if the court orders otherwise. It also does not apply if you or the person served is one of the officials or agencies named in rule 8 (6) (c). An assignee is an agency or person a support order or agreement has been assigned to. If the order or agreement was assigned, you must serve the assignee as if it were a party. You may ask to change child support set out in an order under the Divorce Act (Canada). If that support was recalculated under section 39.1 of the Family Law Act in the 35 days before you file, there is one more step. You must also serve the motion papers on the Director of the Family Responsibility Office. Do you ask to change a final support order or a support agreement? Then you must serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1) with your motion. You do not need one if your only support claim is for child support in the table amount. But you do need one if the motion also makes a property claim. You also need one if it claims exclusive possession (sole use) of the matrimonial home and its contents. With the financial statement, you must serve other papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They include the papers in rule 13 (3.1) and a current list of what is owed from the Family Responsibility Office. If you ask to change or cancel arrears, you must also serve proof of your income for each of those years. This is your income tax return with your notice of assessment, and any notice of reassessment. If those notices are unavailable for a year, use the Canada Revenue Agency's Income and Deductions printout with the return instead. If you do not have to file a tax return and chose not to because of the Indian Act (Canada), serve some other proof of income. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with those papers. File the certificate no later than six days before a case conference. If your motion is not on consent, you may use an affidavit instead of Parts C and D of Form 15. It must have the facts the court needs to make the order you ask for. Rules 14 (18) and (19) also apply to that affidavit. If the parties and any assignee all agree to the change, the steps are different. The parties must then file a consent motion to change (Form 15C) and the other papers rule 15 (17) lists. If the agreed change is to a final support order or support agreement, each party must file a financial statement with Form 15C. This does not apply if you both say in the form that you agree not to. If the agreed change is only about child support, they must file Form 15D and the papers rule 15 (18) lists. With Form 15D, no financial statements need to be served or filed.
yourDeadline:
Serve and file your motion to change (Form 15). Include all required attachments, a blank response (Form 15B) and a blank consent (Form 15C). If you ask to change decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, include the papers rule 35.1 requires. Serve it by special service, not regular service. Someone other than you must serve it, unless the court orders otherwise. If the other party and any assignee agree to the change, you do not serve a motion to change. Instead the parties file a consent motion to change (Form 15C), with the papers the rule lists. If only child support is changing, use Form 15D. If you ask to change support, serve and file your financial statement with the motion. You do not need one if the only support claim is child support in the table amount. Add a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). If the order or agreement was assigned, serve the assignee as if it were a party.

If the order is a support order under the Family Law Act, you cannot apply to vary it within six months after it was made. The same is true within six months after the last decision on an application to vary it. The court can give permission (leave). The six months are counted under the Legislation Act, 2006. They end on the day with the same number as the start day. If that month has no such day, they end on its last day.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take another step in the case. The one exception is booking a case conference. The court can order otherwise on a motion. The rule counts the 45 days from when the case started. It says nothing more exact for a motion to change.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). It is 30 days after they get your motion and its papers, if they live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, it is 60 days. If they do neither, you may file a motion form (Form 14B) asking the court to make the order you asked for in your papers. userQuestion: My ex wants to change our final order — what do I have to do, and by when?
whatsHappening: Another party has served you with a motion to change a final order or agreement. The rules give you two ways to reply. Which one you use depends on whether you agree to the change. Your time to reply depends on where you live.
whatToDoNext: Do you disagree with the change, or want the court to make an added or different change? Then you must serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B), with all required attachments. You must do this within 30 days after you get the motion to change and its papers, if you live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, the limit is 60 days. Do you agree to the change, or have you and the other party agreed to a different change? Then you must fill in the parts of the consent motion to change (Form 15C) that apply to you. Within the same 30 or 60 days, you must return a signed copy to the party making the motion. You must also give a copy of the signed consent to the assignee, if there is one. An assignee is an agency or person a support order or agreement has been assigned to. If the order or agreement was assigned, you must serve your response on the assignee as if it were a party. You may use an affidavit to give the facts that support your side. It can replace Parts C and D of Form 15B, or add to them. Rules 14 (18) and (19) apply to that affidavit. Does the motion ask to change a final support order or a support agreement? Then you must serve and file a financial statement within the same time as your response or consent. Your response (Form 15B) must be served and filed at the same time as the financial statement. This is subject to rule 13 (1.3). Under it, a party making a claim does not have to file a financial statement in one case. That is when their only support claim is for child support in the table amount. That does not apply if there is also a property claim. It also does not apply if there is a claim for exclusive possession (sole use) of the matrimonial home and its contents. The motion may not need a financial statement, but your response may ask to change a support order or support agreement. If so, the financial statement rules apply to you too. With a financial statement, you must serve other papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They include the papers in rule 13 (3.1) and a current list of what is owed from the Family Responsibility Office. If you are the one asking to change or cancel arrears, you must also serve proof of your income for each of those years. This is your income tax return with your notice of assessment, and any notice of reassessment. If those notices are unavailable for a year, use the Canada Revenue Agency's Income and Deductions printout with the return instead. If you do not have to file a tax return and chose not to because of the Indian Act (Canada), serve some other proof of income. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with those papers. File the certificate no later than four days before a case conference. Your response may make a claim about decision-making responsibility or parenting time, net family property, a matrimonial home, or support. If it does, the clerk may give you an automatic order (Form 8.0.1). If the clerk gives you one, you must serve it on every other party. Serve it promptly, and no later than seven days after it is issued.
yourDeadline:
If you do not agree, or want the court to make an added or different change, serve and file a response (Form 15B). If you agree, return a signed consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion. Give a copy to any assignee. You have 30 days after the day you receive the motion to change and its supporting documents. It is 60 days if you do not live in Canada or the United States. The motion may ask to change support, or your response may ask for a support change. If so, your financial statement is due in the same time. Serve the papers the rule lists with it. Examples are the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) and a current schedule of arrears from the Family Responsibility Office. Add a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). Your response may ask for its own change to parenting, property or support. If the clerk then issues an automatic order, serve it promptly, and no later than 7 days after it is issued. Where the information program applies, your certificate must be filed before you serve the response. This is explained below. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take any step in the case except booking a case conference. The rule's other exception is for an answer. It does not mention a response to a motion to change. So where the program applies, attend it and file your certificate before your response is due. Or ask the court on a motion to excuse you. The rule counts the 45 days from when the case started. It says nothing more exact for a motion to change.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: Say you do not serve and file a response, or return a consent, as required. Then these things apply, unless a court orders otherwise. You do not get notice of more steps in the case, except service of an order. You cannot take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without you, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial. The party making the motion may also file a motion form (Form 14B) asking the court to make the order they asked for in their papers. They cannot do this if an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest and opposes the change. If the motion is opposed, a judge must hold at least one conference. Even after you serve and file a response, the parties and any assignee may still agree before the hearing. They may then go ahead on consent by filing the papers rule 15 (19) lists.

citations.quote: The following rules apply to a party who is served with a motion to change a final order or agreement: 1. If the party does not agree to the change or if the party wants to ask the court to make an additional or a different change to the final order or agreement, the party shall serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B), with all required attachments, within the time set out in clause (10) (a) or (b), as the case may be.

2. If the party agrees to the change or if the parties agree to a different change, the party shall complete the applicable portions of the consent motion to change (Form 15C) and shall, within the time set out in clause (10) (a) or (b), as the case may be, i. return a signed copy of the consent motion to change to the party making the motion, and ii. provide a copy of the signed consent motion to change to the assignee, if any.

The documents referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 of subrule (9) shall be served and filed or returned and provided, (a) no later than 30 days after the party responding to the motion receives the motion to change and the supporting documents, if that party resides in Canada or the United States of America; or (b) no later than 60 days after the party responding to the motion receives the motion to change and the supporting documents, in any other case.
“assignee” means an agency or person to whom a support order or agreement that is the subject of a motion under this rule is assigned under the Family Law Act or the Divorce Act (Canada).

In a motion to change a final order or agreement that has been assigned to an assignee, a party shall, in serving documents under subrule (5) or paragraph 1 of subrule (9), serve the documents on the assignee as if the assignee were also a party.

A party who responds to a motion to change a final order or agreement by serving and filing a response to motion to change (Form 15B) may use an affidavit to provide evidence supporting his or her position instead of completing Parts C and D of the form or in addition to those Parts of the form and, in that case, the affidavit is deemed to be part of the form.
Subrules 14 (18) and (19) apply with necessary changes to an affidavit provided in accordance with subrule (22) or (23).

2. The party responding to the motion shall serve and file a financial statement within the time for serving and filing the response to motion to change (Form 15B) or returning the consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion, as set out in subrule 15 (10). Any response to motion to change (Form 15B) shall be served and filed at the same time as the financial statement.

Subject to subrule (1.3), the following rules respecting financial statements apply if a motion is made under rule 15 requesting a change to a final support order or a support agreement: 1. The party making the motion shall serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1) with the motion to change (Form 15).

If the only claim for support contained in the application, answer or motion is a claim for child support in the amount specified in the table of the applicable child support guidelines, the party making the claim is not required to file a financial statement, unless the application, answer or motion also contains a property claim or a claim for exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents.

Subrules (4) and (4.1), or subrule (4.2), as the case may be, apply with necessary changes if a party makes a motion to change an order or agreement for which the party is not required by this rule to file a financial statement, and the party responding to the motion requests a change to a support order or support agreement.

A party who is required under subrules (4) to (4.3) to serve and file a financial statement shall serve with the financial statement the following information, unless the court orders otherwise: 1. The documents referred to in subrule (3.1). 2. A current schedule of arrears from the Family Responsibility Office.

3. One of the following for each year for which the party is seeking to change or cancel arrears, as proof of the party’s income: i. The party’s income tax return and, A. the party’s notice of assessment and, if any, notice of reassessment, or B. if a notice of assessment and a notice of reassessment are unavailable for the year, a copy of the Income and Deductions printout provided by the Canada Revenue Agency for the party. ii. If the party is not required to and has chosen not to file an income tax return because of the Indian Act (Canada), some other proof of income.

A party who is required to serve documents under subrule (3.1), (3.3), (3.4) or (5.0.1) shall confirm service by, (a) serving a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) together with the documents; and (b) filing the certificate no later than, (i) six days before a case conference, in the case of the applicant or the party making the motion, as the case may be, and (ii) four days before the case conference, in the case of the other party.

This rule applies to a case in which any of the following claims is made, if the claim is made on or after February 1, 2022: 1. A claim respecting decision-making responsibility or parenting time with respect to a child under the Divorce Act (Canada) or Part III of the Children’s Law Reform Act. 2. A claim respecting net family property under Part I of the Family Law Act. 3. A claim respecting a matrimonial home under Part II of the Family Law Act. 4. A claim for support under the Divorce Act (Canada) or Part III of the Family Law Act.
On the making of a claim to which this rule applies, the clerk shall issue an automatic order (Form 8.0.1) and provide it to the party making the claim.

2. If the claim is made in an answer, motion to change a final order or agreement under rule 15 or response to motion to change, the automatic order shall be served promptly after the party receives it from the clerk, but in any event not later than seven days after the automatic order is issued.

The consequences set out in paragraphs 1 to 4 of subrule 1 (8.4) apply, with necessary changes, if a party does not serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B) or return a consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion as required under subrule (9).

the following consequences apply unless a court orders otherwise: 1. The party is not entitled to any further notice of steps in the case, except as provided by subrule 25 (13) (service of order). 2. The party is not entitled to participate in the case in any way. 3. The court may deal with the case in the party’s absence. 4. A date may be set for an uncontested trial of the case.

If a party does not serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B) or return a consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion as required under subrule (9), or if the party’s response is struck out by an order, the party making the motion to change may file a motion form (Form 14B) asking that the court make the order requested in the materials filed by the party, unless an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest in the motion and opposes the change.

Subrule (1) applies, with necessary changes, to a motion to change a final order or agreement under rule 15, unless the motion is proceeding on the consent of the parties and any assignee or is unopposed.
Subject to subrules (1.1) and (1.2), in each case in which an answer is filed, a judge shall conduct at least one conference.

If, at any time after a party has served and filed a response under paragraph 1 of subrule (9) and before the motion to change is heard, the parties and any assignee agree to an order that changes the final order or agreement that is the subject of the motion, the parties may proceed on consent by filing, (a) a consent motion to change (Form 15C);

userQuestion: Our family case is going to trial — what do I have to file before it starts?
whatsHappening: Your family case has been scheduled for trial, and the trial has not started yet. A case can be scheduled for trial only after a settlement conference, or if a judge ordered that it be scheduled for trial. Some papers are due before the trial starts. Which ones are yours can depend on whether you are the applicant or a respondent.
whatToDoNext: If you are the applicant, you must serve and file a trial record at least 20 days before the trial starts, or before the trial sitting if that is earlier. It must have a table of contents and the documents the rule lists. They include the application, answer and reply, if any, any agreed statement of facts, and any temporary order about a matter still in dispute. If you are a respondent, you may serve, file and add any listed document that is not already in the trial record, no later than seven days before the trial starts. Your last financial statement may be more than 40 days old by the start of the trial or trial sitting, whichever is earlier. If so, you must serve and file an update no later than 30 days before that date. If nothing has changed, the update is an affidavit saying the last statement has not changed and is still true. If the changes are only minor, it is an affidavit with details of the changes. For any other change, it is a new financial statement. If there is a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, each party must serve and file a net family property statement (Form 13B) no later than 30 days before the trial or trial sitting, whichever is earlier. If you already served one and it has not changed, you may instead serve and file an affidavit by then saying it has not changed and is still true. This does not apply if the property claim arises within a claim about a family arbitration, arbitration agreement or arbitration award. If you want a witness to give evidence in court, or to be questioned and bring documents or other things, you must serve them with a summons to witness (Form 23). A summons to a witness outside Ontario under the Interprovincial Summonses Act uses Form 23A instead. The summons and the witness fee must be served at least seven days before the witness must be in court or at a questioning. For a person outside Ontario who will not come here to be questioned, the court may set a different notice time. Unless the court orders otherwise, the summons must be served by leaving a copy with the witness. For a child, or a person who is or appears to be mentally incapable in respect of an issue in the case, a copy also goes to certain others, as rule 6 (3) (a) sets out. Someone other than you must serve it, unless the court orders otherwise or an exception for officials and agencies applies. The witness fee includes $50 for each day the witness is needed, plus travel money. It also includes $100 a night for meals and a place to stay, if the witness lives outside the city or town of the trial and must stay overnight. To call the other party as a witness, you may serve them with a summons, or serve their lawyer with a notice of intention to call them at least 10 days before the trial starts. You may ask the court for an order letting a party or witness give evidence by affidavit or another way that does not need them to come in person. That evidence may be used at trial only if it follows that order and is served at least 30 days before the trial starts. It must also be evidence that would have been allowed if the person gave it in court. A supplementary report by a litigation expert must be signed by the expert, served on all other parties and filed. This must be done at least 30 days before the trial starts, or at least 14 days before in a child protection case.
yourDeadline:
If you are the applicant, serve and file a trial record with a table of contents and the documents the rule lists. Do this at least 20 days before the start of the trial or of the trial sitting, whichever is earlier. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it. Separately, an offer to settle counts under the costs rule in r. 24 (12) only if it is made at least 7 days before the trial. It must also stay open until the trial starts.

If you are the respondent and want to add a document that is not already in the trial record, serve and file it. Do this at least 7 days before the start of the trial. Only papers of the kinds listed for the trial record can be added. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Update your financial information by serving and filing an affidavit or a new financial statement. Do this at least 30 days before the start of the trial or of the trial sitting, whichever is earlier. This applies only if your last financial statement would be more than 40 days old by then. That is the start of the trial or trial sitting, whichever is earlier. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If there is a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, serve and file a net family property statement (Form 13B), or an affidavit that your last one has not changed. Do this at least 30 days before the start of the trial or of the trial sitting, whichever is earlier. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If your litigation expert has a supplementary report, serve it on all other parties and file it, signed by the expert. Do this at least 30 days before the start of the trial. In a child protection case it is 14 days. The parties cannot change this time by agreement. It can be extended only by an order made at the settlement conference. The trial judge or the judge managing the case can order otherwise.

If you need a witness, serve a summons to witness (Form 23) with the witness fee by leaving it with the witness personally. Do this at least 7 days before the day the witness must be in court or at a questioning. Someone other than you must serve it, unless the court orders otherwise. The court can also order another way of serving it. The opposing party may have a lawyer. To call that party as a witness, you can instead serve their lawyer with a notice of intention to call them. Do that at least 10 days before the trial starts. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If the court ordered that evidence be given by affidavit or another way without coming to court, serve that evidence. Do this at least 30 days before the start of the trial. If you do not, it cannot be used at trial. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
whatHappensAfter: A summons stays in effect until the witness has given evidence or been questioned. It ends sooner if it is set aside, if notice is given that it is no longer needed, or if the witness is otherwise no longer needed. If a summons is no longer needed, the party who served it must give the witness written notice as soon as possible, with the reason. If a witness who was served properly does not obey the summons, the court may issue a warrant for arrest (Form 32B) if the witness must be present.

(ii) if the person is or appears to be mentally incapable in respect of an issue in the case, with the person and with the guardian of the person’s property or, if none, with the Public Guardian and Trustee, (iii) if the person is a child, with the child and with the child’s lawyer, if any,
Special service of the following documents shall be carried out only by a method set out in clause (3) (a), unless the court orders otherwise: 1. A notice of contempt motion. 2. A summons to witness.
Subject to subrule (4.2), special service of the following documents shall be carried out by a person other than the party required to serve the document:

Subrule (4.1) does not apply if, (a) the party required to serve the document or the person being served is a person referred to in clause 8 (6) (c) (officials, agencies, etc.); or (b) the court orders otherwise.
A person summoned as a witness shall be paid, for each day that the person is needed in court or to be questioned, (a) $50 for coming to court or to be questioned; (b) travel money in the amount of,
(c) $100 per night for meals and overnight stay, if the person does not live in the city or town where the trial is held and needs to stay overnight.

A party who wishes to call an opposing party as a witness may have the opposing party attend, (a) by serving a summons under subrule (3) on the opposing party; or (b) by serving on the opposing party’s lawyer, at least 10 days before the start of the trial, a notice of intention to call the opposing party as a witness.

A party may request that the court make an order under clause 1 (7.2) (i) permitting the evidence of a party or witness to be heard by affidavit or another method not requiring the party or witness to attend in person.

Evidence at trial by affidavit or another method not requiring a party or witness to attend in person may be used only if, (a) the use is in accordance with an order under clause 1 (7.2) (i); (b) the evidence is served at least 30 days before the start of the trial; and (c) the evidence would have been admissible if given by the party or witness in court.

Any supplementary report by a litigation expert must be signed by the expert, and shall be served on all other parties and filed, (a) at least 30 days before the start of the trial; or (b) in a child protection case, at least 14 days before the start of the trial.

A summons to witness remains in effect until the witness has given evidence or been questioned, unless notice is given under subrule (5.1), the summons is set aside under subrule (9) or the presence of the witness is otherwise no longer required.

If a summons becomes unnecessary before a witness gives evidence or is questioned, the party who served the summons on the witness shall, as soon as possible, give to the witness written notice of that fact and of the reason why the summons has become unnecessary.

The court may issue a warrant for arrest (Form 32B) to bring a witness before the court if, (a) the witness has been served as subrule (3) requires, but has not obeyed the summons; and (b) it is necessary to have the witness present in court or at a questioning.

userQuestion: There is a support order but the payments are not being made — who enforces it?
whatsHappening: Ontario has a Director of the Family Responsibility Office. The Director's job is to enforce support orders filed in the Director's office. This applies when the order, and any support deduction order that goes with it, are filed there. The Director pays what is collected to the person it is owed to. The clerk or registrar of the court that made a support order must file it there promptly once it is signed.
whatToDoNext: While a support order is filed there, only the Director may enforce it. The one exception is someone given the Director's powers under section 4 of the Act. The Director may refuse to enforce all or part of a filed order in some cases the Act lists. They include an order whose meaning is unclear. They also include when the person owed support has not met reasonable requests for facts the Director needs. An order that was withdrawn from the Director's office may be filed there again at any time. The payor or the recipient does this by signing a written notice. A support order and any support deduction order that goes with it must be filed again together. Whoever files or refiles a support order there must give notice right away. It goes to the clerk at any court office where the recipient is enforcing the order. It can be sent by mail or email. It can also be sent online, through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. A person owed support who files the order there may have started to enforce it on their own. If the Director asks, they must hand that over to the Director. A payment order is a temporary or final order to pay money to another person, such as a support order. It does not include a provisional order. The Family Law Rules list ways to enforce a payment order. Who uses these ways depends on where the order is. While a support order is filed in the Director's office, only the Director may use them, apart from the exception above. If it is not filed there, the person owed the money may. The ways include a request for a financial statement, seizure and sale, and garnishment. A default hearing can also be used if the order is a support order. When the Director enforces an order, the rules for the person the order favours apply to the Director. Other orders may be enforced in three ways. They are a writ to seize property for a time, a contempt order, and naming a receiver. All of these are in addition to other ways the law provides.
whatHappensAfter: Using one way to enforce a support order does not stop other ways at the same time or at other times. The Director may enforce arrears that built up before the order was filed there. If an order is withdrawn, the Director must stop enforcing it. But the Director may keep enforcing to collect arrears owed to an agency from a past assignment.

A support order or support deduction order that has been withdrawn under subsection (1) or that has been deemed to have been withdrawn under subsection 7 (3) may be filed in the office of the Director at any time by a written notice signed by either the payor or the recipient.

A support order cannot be filed under subsection (6) unless the related support deduction order, if any, is also filed and a support deduction order cannot be filed under subsection (6) unless the related support order is also filed.

“payment order” means a temporary or final order, but not a provisional order, requiring a person to pay money to another person, including, (a) an order to pay an amount under Part I or II of the Family Law Act or the corresponding provisions of a predecessor Act, (b) a support order,

A person who files or refiles a support order in the Director’s office shall immediately give notice of the filing by, (a) sending it by mail or email to the clerk at any court office where the recipient is enforcing the order; or (b) submitting it through the Justice Services Online website or through the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available.

A recipient who files a support order in the Director’s office shall, on the Director’s request, assign to the Director any enforcement that the recipient has started, and then the Director may continue with the enforcement as if the Director had started it.
An order that has not been obeyed may, in addition to any other method of enforcement provided by law, be enforced as provided by subrules (3) and (4).

A payment order may be enforced by, (a) a request for a financial statement (subrule 27 (1)); ... (d) seizure and sale (rule 28); (e) garnishment (rule 29); (f) a default hearing (rule 30), if the order is a support order;

An order other than a payment order may be enforced by, (a) a writ of temporary seizure of property (subrule 28 (10)); (b) a contempt order (rule 31); and (c) the appointment of a receiver under section 101 of the Courts of Justice Act.

If the Director enforces an order under the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, anything in these rules relating to enforcement by the person in whose favour the order was made applies to the Director.
Enforcement of a support order or support deduction order by one means does not prevent enforcement by other means at the same time or different times.
The Director may enforce the payment of arrears of support under a support order although they were incurred before the order was filed in the Director’s office or before July 2, 1987.
The Director shall cease enforcement of an order upon its withdrawal from the Director’s office.

If there are arrears owing to an agency referred to in subsection 14 (1) from a past assignment, the Director may continue to enforce the support order and related support deduction order, if any, to collect the arrears owed to the agency, even if the payor and recipient have withdrawn the orders under this section.
